Imagine you're building a data agent to answer questions about an enterprise data warehouse. Ideally, you'd develop and test it against production data, but access restrictions and data sensitivity make that difficult – especially when the engineers building the agent sit outside the team that owns the data. Even with access, a live warehouse is a poor test track: Catalog descriptions are often incomplete or contradicted by institutional knowledge in docs and chat threads; there’s no verified answer key across its thousands of tables; and you can't systematically vary the complexity of the data and documents to see where the agent breaks. So teams often test on toy datasets and hope the agent holds up in production.

Other disciplines test differently. Automobile designers study aerodynamics by putting a scale model in a wind tunnel, which reproduces the airflow forces that matter while ignoring surface details like paint and badges. A shape that performs well in the tunnel performs well on the road because the tunnel preserves the physical properties the shape responds to.

Data agents need a wind tunnel too: a synthetic data estate (the databases, documents, and chat history where a company's knowledge lives) with the same structure and causal behavior as a real organization, while synthesizing every name, number, and document. Most Gemini prototypes start the same way. You grab an API key from Google AI Studio, then paste it into your coding agent to start building a prototype. That speed is the point, and shouldn’t be slowed down.

The trouble starts later, when the prototype gets real users and the key comes along unchanged. By then it usually isn't one key. Every developer has their own, often several, sitting in .env files, shell profiles and chat threads. The app has one more, baked into its config.

For example, imagine an account that normally spends $180 a month. One of those keys ends up in a public repo, a Slack channel or a mobile app bundle. Automated scrapers find it within minutes and use it to run large workloads. By the time the first billing alert arrives, the bill is in the tens of thousands. How we’re addressing safety risks of distillation and lessons we’ve learned for strengthening safeguards across the industry.

As frontier AI models become more capable, safeguards play an increasingly important role in how they can be used responsibly. Adversarial distillation creates a path for bad actors to reproduce these capabilities without appropriate safeguards. An actor may use a frontier model’s outputs without authorization to train another model with similar capabilities, then deploy it without comparable protections. For instance, an adversary might distill a model’s cyber capabilities and use the resulting model to help carry out cyberattacks that the original model would have refused to assist with or that its safeguards would have blocked.

We’re sharing how OpenAI detects and disrupts adversarial distillation, how we’ve strengthened protections for our models’ protected reasoning, and what we’ve learned that can help strengthen defenses across the industry.

Our approach to adversarial distillation combines adversarial testing, model training, classifiers, and API-level protections with investigations into coordinated attempts to extract model capabilities. These updated safeguards align more closely with those we use for biology and cybersecurity.

We’re introducing MedChemBench, a benchmark that evaluates AI models on reasoning tasks drawn from medicinal chemistry research. It tests whether models can connect a molecule’s structure with experimental evidence to explain results, compare compounds, and predict their properties. Building AI that can reliably support this work is one step towards helping scientists develop better medicines.

One of the hardest parts of this work is that improving one property of a molecule can make another worse. A compound might act strongly against a disease related protein but be poorly absorbed or break down too quickly in the body. Medicinal chemists work through these tradeoffs by designing, making, and testing related compounds, then deciding what to try next. As the volume of data handled by AI continues to grow, memory technology for storing and processing that data efficiently is evolving ever faster. items.title: How we’re putting one of quantum mechanics’ deepest features to the test at scale.
items.summary: Google Quantum AI research proves contextuality powers quantum algorithms at scale. See how our processor beat classical limits. Get the details.
items.excerpt:
Today, in new research published on the cover of Science, Google Quantum AI demonstrated that contextuality — a quantum property scientists believe powers certain quantum algorithms — survives at scale on our quantum processor.

What gives quantum computers their unique power? While entanglement usually gets the spotlight, theory suggests that a deeper quantum property called contextuality may power certain quantum algorithms. In simple terms, contextuality means a system’s properties aren’t fixed in advance; what you measure depends on which other compatible measurements you make alongside it.

Until recently, this effect had mostly been shown in small systems of just a few particles. Our paper in Science now demonstrates this at scale on our quantum processor. Using it, our qubits won a well-known coordination game 98.3% of the time, beating the 88.9% classical limit, and outperformed constrained classical strategies in tasks spanning up to 105 qubits.

These tests also serve as a sensitive new method to catch subtle hardware errors, helping pave the way for real-world applications like chemistry and materials science. Read the full Google Research blog post to learn more.

When an agent connects to dozens or even hundreds of tools, sending every full parameter schema on every request adds up fast. Tool Retrieval lets your agent keep its full tool library on standby and load parameter schemas only when the current task needs them.

When the model needs a tool, it asks for it by name, the API loads the full schema, and the model calls the function, all inside the same request.

The speed of development in large open-source projects has always been limited by code review, not code generation. Even as coding agents get better at writing code, they do not accelerate development on their own. This is especially true of patches to the Linux kernel. Without a way to build trust in proposed changes, more generated code simply piles up in front of the same small group of human maintainers. Some of those patches are solid changes, just written faster; many others are plausible-looking "AI slop" sent by contributors who do not fully understand the systems they are modifying. And the influx of AI-generated security reports, many of which are duplicates or inaccurate, only adds to maintainers’ load.

Linux runs billions of Android phones, most cloud providers, and nearly every supercomputer. It spans more than 35 million lines of code, and over 85,000 changes land every year. Automated build bots and fuzzers like Syzkaller catch build errors and crashes, but code review has always been the main way to guarantee the stability and safety of the kernel. Every day, maintainers read hundreds and hundreds of proposed patches by hand to catch memory leaks, deadlocks, race conditions, and security bugs.

In June we introduced the Open Knowledge Format (OKF), an open specification that provides plain markdown and YAML to give agents the context they need. In July, v0.2 added trust signals: provenance, trust, freshness, lifecycle, and attestation.

In production, bundles move between organizations, multiple agents edit the same corpus, and independent tools need to read a bundle the same way. Released today, OKF v0.3 adds precise conformance rules, trust tiers that keep pace with agent edits, self-describing bundles with licensing, safe ways to retire and move knowledge, a stable extension model, and a clear versioning policy. However, the core idea behind OKF stays the same: type is still the only required field, and your existing bundles keep working.

We're also launching OKF use cases, which are community guides for using OKF alongside other industry standards, and two agent skills that let coding agents write and read OKF bundles. I watched the discussion on agentic loops grow louder over the past few months. But for me, the reality is simpler: prompt engineering has shifted from individual tasks to systems design, and the harness around the model (not the model itself) is now my primary constraint in software engineering. In this article, I'll show you how to build and verify those harnesses so you can move from single-turn instructions to durable agentic loops in Google Antigravity.

You can categorize the work that we give to our agents into five distinct tiers, scaling from a quick question up through Agile tasks, stories, and epics to a continuous system:

A simple question: This does not require an agent; an assistant can answer it.

A task / idea: This is one where a single prompt can zero-shot it. Use Google AI Studio to quickly transform ideas to functional prototypes.

An app / larger feature / story: The kind of work that required weekly planning and splitting into subtasks before AI. Use loops for execution and full-featured agents, like Google Antigravity. This tier is also where your steering moves upstream: You lock in the spec, the plan, and the executable tests before any loop runs.

A project / epic: A few features that make a cohesive story when connected. Loops here might help with planning too. This is also where one needs to go beyond simple turn-based prompting.

In our latest installment of the Ask a Scientist series, a Google DeepMind research scientist explains the potential behind our AlphaGenome and AlphaGenome Atlas tools.

Your genome is your body’s instruction manual: the blueprint that informs how your body functions. It contains 3 billion base pairs of DNA. Because this DNA is responsible in part for switching genes on and off, it could be the difference between developing a disease and avoiding one. Determining which DNA changes cause diseases (and other outcomes) is like finding a needle in a haystack.

Illustrative. Your genome, one point at a time.

Decoding the DNA sequence is the goal behind AlphaGenome, a model from Google DeepMind. AlphaGenome can take a partial DNA sequence of 1 million base pairs in length, and make thousands of predictions. By comparing these predictions for DNA changes, scientists can find that needle faster.

NVIDIA Announces Financial Results for Third Quarter Fiscal 2027

•Revenue of $115.8 billion, up 103% from a year ago

•Data Center revenue of $107.6 billion, up 110% from a year ago

•Vera Rubin NVL72, the most versatile and advanced computing platform ever built, has shipped

SANTA CLARA, Calif.—Nov. 17, 2026―NVIDIA (NASDAQ: NVDA) today reported revenue for the third quarter ended October 25, 2026, of $115.8 billion, up 20% from the previous quarter and up 103% from a year ago. For the quarter, GAAP and non-GAAP gross margins were 74.8% and 74.9%, respectively. GAAP and non-GAAP earnings per diluted share were $2.70 and $2.68, respectively.

“Our momentum is real. NVIDIA is an exceptional technology leader, powered by the relentless innovation of our people,” said Colette Kress, interim CEO and executive vice president and chief financial officer of NVIDIA. “Vera Rubin is off to an explosive start, our roadmap is on track and our ambition has never been greater.”

In September 2026, NVIDIA’s Board of Directors approved an increase of $150 billion to the company’s share repurchase authorization, without expiration. During the third quarter of fiscal 2027, NVIDIA returned $28.1 billion to shareholders in the form of shares repurchased and cash dividends. As of the end of the third quarter, the company had approximately $227.3 billion remaining under its share repurchase authorization.

NVIDIA will pay its next quarterly cash dividend of $0.25 per share on December 23, 2026, to all shareholders of record on December 2, 2026.
